notes.meaning: Two full years passed after the cupbearer was restored to his office before Pharaoh had his dream. Joseph had to wait patiently in prison until God's appointed time arrived. God used this dream beside the Nile River to begin Joseph's deliverance and lift him into leadership.

Pharaoh saw seven healthy, well-fed cows come up out of the river to graze among the marsh reeds. Because Egypt depended entirely on the Nile for its harvests, cows feeding by the water were a familiar sign of fruitfulness.
Right after the healthy cows, seven thin and sickly cows came out of the Nile and stood beside them on the bank. Their scrawny bodies showed that the river would fail to bring its usual blessing.
The starving cows devoured the seven sleek cows, which woke Pharaoh up in surprise. It was completely unnatural for cows to eat each other, signaling that an extraordinary crisis was ahead.
Pharaoh fell back asleep and had a second dream with a similar pattern. He saw seven plump, healthy heads of grain growing together on a single stalk.
Seven thin heads of grain sprouted up next, dried out and ruined by the scorching east wind. This dry desert wind was known for quickly withering crops across Egypt.
The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven plump ones, and Pharaoh woke up realizing it was a dream. The scene felt so real and vivid that the king knew it carried a serious warning.

In the morning, Pharaoh felt deeply troubled by his dreams, so he summoned all the magicians and wise men of Egypt. These educated men were trained to explain mysterious signs, but none of them could explain what the dreams meant. God kept them from understanding so that His own servant would be called.
When the wise men failed, the chief cupbearer spoke up and admitted his past wrongdoing. He finally remembered Joseph, though he likely spoke up now to gain favor with the troubled king.

The cupbearer explained how Pharaoh had once been angry with him and the chief baker and locked them up under the captain of the guard. He gave the background so the king would understand how he met Joseph.
He told Pharaoh that both he and the baker had dreams on the very same night. Each dream had its own distinct message about what would happen to them.
A young Hebrew servant was in prison with them and listened as they described their dreams. Joseph correctly explained what each man's dream meant.
Everything turned out exactly as the young Hebrew had foretold. The cupbearer got his job back, while the chief baker was executed.

Pharaoh quickly sent for Joseph, and the guards hurried him out of the prison. Joseph shaved his beard and put on clean clothes to respect Egyptian royal customs before appearing before the king. God's timing brought Joseph from a dark pit to the royal court in a single hour.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars propose that the mention of the dungeon was added by an editor to combine two different written sources about Joseph.

notes.meaning: Pharaoh told Joseph that nobody in Egypt could interpret his dream, but he had heard Joseph could understand any dream he heard. The king offered Joseph a great opportunity to make a name for himself.
Joseph answered humbly that he had no power of his own to explain dreams. He gave all the honor to God, saying that God alone would provide Pharaoh with a meaningful answer.

differ.view: Joseph's statement is a prayer or wish for Pharaoh's well-being, because Joseph did not yet know what God was about to reveal.
Joseph speaks with confident faith that anyone who seeks God's guidance will receive an answer that brings peace and welfare.

notes.meaning: Pharaoh began describing his dream to Joseph, setting the scene on the bank of the Nile River. The river was the lifeblood of Egypt, so the vision struck at the heart of the nation's survival.
Pharaoh repeated how seven plump, healthy cows came up out of the river and fed in the marsh grass. These animals pictured rich pasture and plenty of food for the land.
Next, seven wretched, sickly cows came up behind them. Pharaoh emphasized that he had never seen such ugly, starved animals in all of Egypt.
The thin cows ate up the seven healthy cows that had come out first. This unnatural sight disturbed Pharaoh even more as he retold it.

Even after swallowing the fat cows, the thin cows remained just as sickly and starved as before. This detail showed that the coming disaster would completely swallow up any earlier prosperity. Then Pharaoh woke up.
In his second dream, Pharaoh saw seven full, ripe heads of grain growing on a single stalk. This image pointed to a time of bountiful grain harvests across the nation.
Seven withered, empty heads of grain sprouted up after them, dried out by the desert wind. They had no grain inside, only dry husks.
The thin heads swallowed the plump heads, completely destroying them. Pharaoh told Joseph that he had shared all this with his magicians, but none could make sense of it.

Joseph explained that both dreams had the exact same meaning. God was revealing to Pharaoh what He was about to do in Egypt. Even though the Nile watered the land, the one true God controlled the seasons and the future.
Joseph told the king that the seven healthy cows and seven full heads of grain represented seven years of great abundance. Both pictures pointed to the exact same period of plenty.
The seven skinny cows and seven ruined heads of grain stood for seven years of severe famine. This terrible shortage of food would follow right behind the years of harvest.
Joseph repeated that God had shown Pharaoh what He was about to do. In His kindness, God was warning the king ahead of time so Egypt could prepare for the coming famine.
